el-0: Hand and Finger Osteoarthritis: Symptoms, Treatment and Exercises | İhsan Eren
el-1: Hard knobbly lumps and stiffness in your finger joints? What hand osteoarthritis is, how it differs from inflammatory arthritis, and whether exercise helps. Warning signs and six exercises to do at home.
el-3: Have hard, knobbly lumps appeared on your finger joints, and are opening jars, doing up buttons or picking up small things not as easy as they used to be? Hand osteoarthritis is a long-term joint condition that is common especially after the age of 50. It does not go away completely, but with sensible use of your hands, heat and regular movement, pain and stiffness can often be kept under control.

el-10: Joint pain that gets worse with activity, and short-lived morning stiffness.
el-11: Hard, knobbly swellings on the finger joints (Heberden’s and Bouchard’s nodes).
el-12: Swelling and tenderness at the base of the thumb, sometimes a small “step” in the bone.
el-13: Difficulty gripping, pinching and picking up small objects; pain that gets worse if knocked.
el-14: Over time, the joint surfaces become damaged and no longer move as smoothly.
el-15: Age, sex, previous joint injuries and differences in joint shape increase the risk.
el-16: The joints most often affected are those nearest the fingertips, the middle finger joints and the base of the thumb.
el-18: As it is a long-term condition, keeping your hand’s movement and strength is important; move regularly without putting undue strain on the joints.
el-20: If your hands are stiff or aching, use warm water or a hot water bottle; if a joint is swollen and hot, you can use cold.
el-22: You can reduce the load by taking short breaks during long hand tasks such as knitting, computer work or gardening.
el-24: Mainly for base-of-thumb problems, or deformity causing pain and loss of function, referral to a hand therapist can be helpful.
el-25: Six exercises to free up the hands
el-26: Before you start, warm your hand for a few minutes with warm water or a hot water bottle. Do the movements slowly within a pain-free range; if swelling or pain in the finger joints increases, do less.
el-27: Gently straighten your fingers fully, then slowly make a fist. You do not need to squeeze; the aim is to move the finger joints through their full range.
el-28: Touching the fingertips with the thumb
el-29: Touch the tip of your thumb to the tip of each finger in turn, then open your hand and stretch your thumb out as far as you can. The movement should come from the base of the thumb near the wrist.
el-32: Warm your hand first. With your other hand, gently massage the muscle between your thumb and index finger; if you can, move your thumb away from your index finger at the same time.
el-35: Hold a tennis ball or a soft ball lightly with your thumb and fingers. Squeeze gently, then relax. If the pain increases, choose a softer object.
el-36: Rest your forearm on a table with your hand over the edge. Lift your wrist as far as is comfortable, then lower it.
el-37: Rest your forearm on a table. Slowly turn your palm to face up, then down.
el-38: What are the hard lumps on my fingers?
el-39: Hard, knobbly swellings on the joints nearest the fingertips are called Heberden’s nodes, and those on the middle joints Bouchard’s nodes. They are typical signs of hand osteoarthritis.
el-41: According to a Cochrane review, exercise slightly improves hand pain, function and finger stiffness, with an average reduction in pain of half a point on a 0–10 scale. The effect is small and the quality of the evidence is low, but side effects are few and mild. Done regularly, it is a safe way to keep your hands moving.
el-42: Heat is recommended if your hands are stiff or aching, and cold if a joint is swollen or hot. Warming your hand for a few minutes in warm water or with a hot water bottle before exercising can make movement easier.
el-43: How is it different from inflammatory arthritis?
el-44: In hand osteoarthritis, pain usually gets worse with activity and morning stiffness lasts no more than half an hour; at 45 or over, this picture is often enough to make the diagnosis without tests. Soft, warm, puffy swelling of the joints, on the other hand, suggests an inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis and needs assessment by a rheumatologist.
